name: Feedforward Neural Network (FNN)
analogy: Think of it as an assembly line of scoring desks. The first desk reads the raw numbers about a bar, the next desk combines those readings into slightly more abstract judgments, and the last desk turns them into one answer. Information only ever moves forward, never back.

steps.title: Feed in one row of numbers
steps.description: The network receives a single row of numeric features describing one bar. Each number enters its own input slot. The features should be put on comparable scales first, so a price near 19,000 does not drown out a small momentum reading.
steps.inExample: A 5-minute MNQ bar arrives as six scaled numbers: close, relative strength index, volume against average, average true range, distance from the 50-bar average and the 6-bar return.

steps.title: Mix the inputs in the first hidden layer
steps.description: Every input slot is connected to every unit in the first hidden layer. Each unit takes its own weighted blend of all the inputs, so each unit becomes a small detector for one combination of features.
steps.inExample: One unit in the first layer weighs a falling 6-bar return together with a low relative strength index, so it lights up when price has dropped fast and looks oversold.

steps.title: Bend the result with an activation
steps.description: Each blended value passes through a simple bending rule, for example keeping positive values and zeroing negative ones. Without this bend, stacked layers would collapse into one straight-line formula and could never learn curved relationships.
steps.inExample: The oversold detector outputs a strong signal for this bar, while a unit that watches for overbought conditions is switched to zero.

steps.title: Stack more hidden layers
steps.description: The outputs of the first layer become the inputs of the next layer, which blends them again. Later layers combine earlier detectors into broader ideas, such as a heavy-volume oversold drop.
steps.inExample: The second layer combines the oversold detector with a heavy-volume detector into a single unit meaning a sharp, busy sell-off.

steps.title: Produce the answer at the output layer
steps.description: The last layer collapses the final ideas into the answer the task needs. For a direction call that is one probability squeezed between zero and one hundred percent.
steps.inExample: The output unit reads the sell-off idea and returns a 56 percent probability that the close 6 bars later is higher.

steps.title: Learn by being corrected
steps.description: During training, the network compares its answers with what really happened, works out how each connection contributed to the error, and nudges every weight a little in the direction that shrinks the error. This repeats over many passes through the training bars.
steps.inExample: On a training bar that closed lower, the 56 percent answer was too bullish, so the weights behind the sell-off idea are nudged slightly so the next answer on a similar bar is lower.

useFor.task: Direction probability from a table of features
useFor.example: Predicting whether MNQ's close 6 bars (30 minutes) after a 5-minute bar is above that bar's close, using the 35 base features as one row.
Training a small two-layer network on the same walk-forward folds as a tree model to see whether curved feature interactions add anything.
Predicting the next 5-minute bar's high-to-low range in points from recent average true range, volume and time of day, to size stops.
Blending several of the 151 technical indicators into one trend-strength score that a rule-based strategy can threshold.

avoidWhen: The order of the last 60 bars carries the signal; this network sees a flat row and has no sense of sequence, so a recurrent or attention model reads that order directly.
You have only a few thousand rows or need to explain each decision; the network overfits easily and its reasoning is hard to inspect, where a tree model is steadier and easier to audit.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes at 19,240. A small network with two hidden layers, trained on the previous 12 months of bars, is asked whether the close 6 bars (30 minutes) later will be higher.

input.summary: One row of scaled features for the bar that just closed.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 5-minute bar closed, in index points.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; low values mean price has fallen hard recently.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How busy this bar was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: distance from the 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: How far the close sits below its recent average price.

fields.name: return over the last 6 bars
fields.meaning: How much price fell over the previous 30 minutes.

output.summary: One probability and the side it implies.

fields.name: probability the close is higher 6 bars later
fields.meaning: The output unit's answer after the row passes through both hidden layers.

fields.name: call
fields.meaning: The side the probability falls on when the dividing line is 50 percent.

example.reading: 56 percent is a slight lean, not a conviction. Compare it with the share of up-closes in the training bars and with trading costs before acting; a lean this small only pays if the average win clearly exceeds commission and slippage.
